text:
At 3:17 a.m., the bakery was all yeast and silence. Marisol slid the first loaves into the oven and found it again: a worn paperback, *The Borrowers*, resting in the wicker basket by the back door. Every Thursday for six weeks, someone had returned it here instead of the library two blocks over. No name. No card. Just the book, smelling faintly of rain and woodsmoke.

Tonight a folded note was tucked between pages 84 and 85. She wiped her floury hands and opened it. *I can't make it to the library before closing. Please keep it another week. I like knowing it's warm.*

Marisol looked at the basket, then at the tray of cinnamon rolls cooling on the rack. She chose the one with the most icing. She wrapped it in wax paper, tucked the note back into the book, and set both by the door. Then she flipped the sign to OPEN and started the coffee.

At 3:47 a.m. the book was there again. Same one—a battered copy of The Long Winter—resting on the flour bin like it had walked in and made itself comfortable. Every Thursday, without fail. I’d stopped asking who. The regulars were asleep. The mice don’t read.

I wiped my hands and opened the cover. A note, folded twice, smelled faintly of cinnamon. Not my cinnamon. I unfolded it.

You always leave the oven light on. It helps.

That was it. No name. No reason. I stood there with dough stuck to my knuckles, listening to the proof box hum. Outside, a bus sighed past. I thought about the woman who buys a single roll every Friday and never eats it in front of me. I thought about my mother’s handwriting, which this wasn’t.

Then I slid the note into my apron pocket, tucked the book under the register, and pulled the next tray of croissants from the oven.

At 2:40 a.m., while the ovens clicked through their preheat, Marla found the book again. *The Anatomy of Melancholy*, stamped with the county library’s faded crest, sitting on the flour bin like a delivered loaf. Every Thursday. No one saw who left it. The security camera showed only the alley, rain, a shadow that didn’t resolve.

She wiped her hands and opened the cover. This time a note lay against the title page, folded twice. Blue ink, block letters: *You burned the last batch. I did too.* No signature.

Marla read it once. The proofing dough breathed under its cloth. She looked at the alley door, the small window, the dark. Then she slid the note into her apron pocket, set the book on the cooling rack beside the day-old rye, and turned back to the mixer. She poured in the water, started the paddle, and watched the dry flour pull away from the bowl’s sides.

At 3:17 a.m., Marisol heard the walk-in cooler kick on and the proofing cabinet breathe. She slid the first loaves into the oven. In the wicker basket by the back door sat the worn paperback again: *The Borrowers*. For six Thursdays someone had left it here instead of the library two blocks over. The checkout card in back was blank; only a barcode and a coffee ring marked it.

A folded note was tucked between pages 84 and 85. She wiped her hands on her apron and read: *I can’t get to the library before it closes. Please keep it here another week. I like knowing it’s warm.*

She looked at the basket, then at the tray of cinnamon rolls cooling on the rack. She chose the one with the most icing, wrapped it in wax paper, and tucked the note back into the book. She set both by the door. At 4:50 she pulled the loaves, knocked them from their pans, and slid the next tray into the oven.
